about: Ogvaldsnes (Avaldsnes on Karmoy), the lord's farm on the Karmsund, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/ogvaldsnes.md, the spine, realms/norway.md and peoples/norse.md. A draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not verified; (saga) marks what rests only on Snorri, about 1230. Local flags begin og_. Woven into the region danes_norway on 7 Oct 2026 by the region's weaver: ties made to run both ways, people named in ties made real in their own ports or pointed at the right id, stories given beats and cards in the other ports, and the region's cards (encounters/danes_norway_793.json) named in the sites' 'do' lists.

ports.summary: Ogvaldsnes is a great farm on a ness of the island Kormt, at the narrowest part of the sound that every ship on the coast road must use. It is a hall and a household, not a town: there is no market, no toll house and no coin, and a stranger trades with the lord or his man, by gift and by leave, with silver on the scale. A merchant comes for iron, soapstone pots, whetstones, down, a walrus tusk when the northern men have passed, and whatever the young men brought home from west over the sea; he brings grain, malt, glass, fine cloth and the Frankish blades he is forbidden to sell.
ports.seasons: Ships go into the water after the first day of summer and come out before the winter nights; nobody sails the coast in the dark months. The young men are away from sowing to harvest, so high summer is a quiet farm of women, old men and thralls, and autumn is the time of feasts, home-comings and things for sale. The tide hardly moves the sound: a hand's breadth at neaps, a forearm at springs.

history.text: About this time a great man is laid in the mound by the farm later called Flaghaug, with a neck ring of gold, weapons and Roman vessels of silver and bronze. In the game's years the mound stands whole and nobody knows what is in it.
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes'; Nordvegen History Centre (avaldsnes.info/en/informasjon/); the year is the middle of 'the 200s'

history.text: Between about 680 and 750 a ship grave is made on the island, called the oldest in the North. Which mound is meant is not said (?).
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes'; the year is the middle of the range

history.text: In the summer a lord is laid in an oak ship some twenty-seven metres long under the Great Mound north of the farm, with a smaller boat, a horse, a sledge, two Frankish swords, a gold arm ring, gaming pieces of amber and glass, a cake of wax marked with a cross and a feather sealed in tin.
history.source: Nordvegen History Centre, Storhaug (avaldsnes.info/en/informasjon/storhaug/); the year from tree rings

history.text: Three ships of Northmen from Hordaland, the next land north of here, come to Portland. The king's reeve takes them for traders and is killed.

Between 790 and 795 a second man is buried in a boat of some fifteen metres under the Green Mound at Bo, with a fine glass beaker, hooped vessels, turned bowls, tapestry and bedding. The game puts the burial in the autumn of 794.
history.source: no.wikipedia 'Gronhaug' (tree-ring dates published 2009); the choice of 794 is the game's

history.text: By tradition in this year, by most scholars in the 880s, Harald Fairhair beats the kings of the west in Hafrsfjord, a day's sail south, and the farm becomes his. That he made it his chief seat is a modern claim: his own poet does not name it.
history.source: Haraldskvaedi (Thorbjorn hornklofi); en.wikipedia 'Battle of Hafrsfjord'; chronicle_793.json 872-hafrsfjord; dossier section 8

history.text: About this year King Harald dies, having dwelt in old age on his great farms, this one among them, and is laid under a mound at Haugar on the sound.
history.source: Heimskringla, Harald Harfager's saga 40, 45 (saga); Nordvegen History Centre

history.text: The sons of Eric land on the island. King Hakon meets them on the heights among the old mounds and Guthorm Ericsson falls. The ground is afterwards called the Blood Heath.
history.source: Heimskringla, Hakon the Good's saga 20 (saga; Laing's margin says 950); en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes'

history.text: King Olaf Tryggvason keeps Easter here with three hundred and sixty men and a bishop. The sorcerer Eyvind Kelda and his crew, blinded in their own mist, are taken and left bound on a skerry that the flood tide covers. That spring an old one-eyed guest keeps the king awake with tales of King Ogvald and his cow.
About now the workshop ground south of the farm, where iron was forged, grain dried and salt boiled since about the year 200, goes out of use.
history.source: Nordvegen History Centre, research page (avaldsnes.info/en/forskning/), after the Royal Manor Project's dig of 2011-2012

history.text: King Olaf Haraldsson forbids corn, malt and meal to go from the south to the north. Late in the summer his bailiff Thorir Sel seizes the whole cargo of Asbjorn Sigurdsson of Halogaland and takes his good striped sail in swap for an old one.

On the Thursday of Easter week Asbjorn strikes off Thorir Sel's head at the king's table. On the Sunday Erling Skjalgsson of Sola comes with nearly fifteen hundred men and frees him. Asbjorn is named bailiff in the dead man's place and never comes back to serve.
The church law for the west is set at Moster, a short sail north: no trade or loading on Sundays and feasts, no meat on Fridays.
history.source: realms/norway.md (the Kuli stone and the Gulathing law for the substance)

history.text: Cnut comes with his fleet and is taken as king. On the twenty-first day of December Erling Skjalgsson is killed off Bokn, at the south end of the sound.
King Olaf's body is taken up and he is held a saint. His feast, the twenty-ninth of July, is kept on the sound from now on.
About three hundred ships sail for England with King Harald Sigurdsson. Twenty-four come home.

eras.text: The old lord of the ness is alive and failing; nobody will be surprised by a second mound. His sister's son Thorleif has the ship and, more and more, the hall. In the summer of 793 the young men are west over the sea, and from the hay moon they are home with things no farm has a use for: silver cut from a shrine, a box of painted skins, two English boys.

The Green Mound is new turf on the ridge beside the old one. Thorleif holds the hall. Every spring the ship goes west and every autumn the benches are full of men with something to sell and a story that leaves most of it out. Thralls of the islands' speech carry the water. A Frank is asked about blades before he is asked his name.

The lords of the ness in these years have no names that anyone wrote down. The farm is the same: the hall, the forge, the boats on the strand, the lord's man at the water in the morning. From the 840s there is a ship-fort at Dyflin, and Irish silver, Irish wives and Irish thralls come up the coast road with the home-coming ships.

The king's farm. After Hafrsfjord the hall is Harald's and a steward keeps it for him; the lord's gift becomes the king's due. Chiefs who will not have a king sell up and go west, and the steward counts heads at five ounces of silver for every man bound for Iceland. In his old age the king himself sits here some winters, heavy and slow, with too many sons.

Eric, and then Hakon, who was fostered in England and keeps his Fridays quietly. The west has one law at the Gula thing. Beacons stand ready on the heights. In 953 they burn: Eric's sons land on the island itself, and afterwards the heath among the old mounds has a new name.

Hard years first: under Harald Greycloak it snows at midsummer and a sack of rye is worth more than its weight in whetstones. Then Jarl Hakon and good seasons. The old feasts are kept at the stone as they always were, and a Christian guest is wise to praise the ale and say nothing.

King Olaf Tryggvason. A heathen crew is offered the first signing or no sailing. Sacrifice is forbidden, the mounds are looked at with a new eye, and a small wooden church goes up beside the hall (saga) (?). At Easter 998 the king feasts here with a bishop and the sound is full of ships.

The jarls rule for the Danish king, and on the spot the great man is Erling Skjalgsson of Sola, a day south. Fifteen easy years: English pennies in every purse, weighed all the same, and nobody asks a skipper his faith twice.

King Olaf Haraldsson and his bailiffs. Thorir Sel, low-born and well dressed, comes down to the strand each morning to ask who commands and what the errand is. From 1022 no corn may go north; from 1024 no loading on a Sunday or a feast. In 1028 Cnut's silver has done its work and the king is gone.

The worst years. Svein and his mother Alfiva rule for Cnut: a room across every outbound ship is the king's, nobody leaves without leave, and in a suit one Dane's oath outweighs ten of the country's. From 1031 the dead King Olaf is a saint, and pilgrims begin to pass north.

Magnus, then Harald Sigurdsson. The farm is one of the king's many and the bailiff's word is the king's. After about 1055 the king's own penny is two parts copper: take weighed silver or goods. In the summer of 1066 every farm on the sound sends a man to England, and in the autumn the widows have things to sell.

sites.name: The strand under the farm
sites.see: A grey shingle beach in a narrow sound, ships drawn up bow first with their striped ship-tents pitched ashore beside them. Behind, a turf slope climbs to the long roof of the hall and a tall leaning stone; across the water the mainland is a low dark line. Oystercatchers, the knock of a mallet, peat smoke, tar and wet kelp. In the morning an old man walks down the path to ask who commands.
sites.source: Heimskringla, Saint Olaf's saga 123 (saga, of 1022): ships lie below the farm, crews under ship-tents, the lord's man comes down in the morning. Tide range from Research/water_levels/north_and_norway.md. No jetty is known before the 1100s

sites.name: The hall on the ness
sites.see: One long room under a turf roof, a fire down the middle and smoke hanging in the rafters. Benches run along both walls with the high seat in the middle of the north side; shields and a striped sail hang behind it. Women with keys at their belts carry ale; thralls who speak the islands' tongue keep the fire. It smells of smoke, wet wool, dogs and boiled meat, and somebody is always halfway through a story.
sites.source: Post holes of Viking Age buildings south of the church (Royal Manor Project, 2011-2012): what the hall of 793 looked like is not known, and this is the ordinary hall of peoples/norse.md. The high seat and ante-room are Saint Olaf's saga 124 (saga, of 1023). Gaming pieces of amber and glass lay in the mound of 779

sites.name: The lord's store
sites.see: A squat log house on stone footings beside the hall, its door bound with iron and a woman's key in the lock. Inside, in the half dark: soapstone pots nested in hay, bundles of grey whetstones, bar iron, sacks of down, corn bins, and on one shelf the odd things from over the sea. A folding scale hangs by the door. This is as near to a market as the place has: you deal with whoever holds the key.
sites.source: No market is recorded here (dossier section 4): goods changed hands with the lord or his bailiff. 'Great corn stacks' at the farm in 1022 (Saint Olaf's saga 123, saga). The goods are the region's (realms/norway.md), not proven for this farm. Scales in women's graves: peoples/norse.md 3 (?)

sites.name: The workshop ground
sites.see: A trampled yard south of the hall, black with charcoal. A smith works under an open lean-to with a boy at the bellows; beyond him grain dries on a clay floor over a slow fire, and at the shore a thrall feeds driftwood under a pan of sea water crusted white. Hammer on iron, the hiss of the quench, the bitter smell of burnt seaweed and hot salt.
sites.source: The workshop area: forging, handicraft, grain drying and salt making, in use about 200 to 1000 (Nordvegen History Centre, research page)

sites.name: The boat shore
sites.see: North of the strand a long low boat-house of turf and stone opens straight on the water, a hull on rollers inside it and another half built beside it under the sky. Split oak planks lie stacked with sticks between them; a trough steams. A lean man sights along a strake and says nothing. Wood shavings, tar pots, wool yarn for caulking, and the sound of an adze that never hurries.
sites.source: The ships in the mounds: an oak ship of about 27 m (779) and a boat of about 15 m built about 780 (avaldsnes.info Storhaug; no.wikipedia 'Gronhaug'). Shipwrights are inferred from them (dossier section 3). Boat-houses are common on this coast from before the game's years; none has been reported at the farm itself (?). story/ships_793.json lists this port as a building place

sites.name: The Great Mound
sites.see: A round green hill made by hands, fifty paces across and three men high, on the ridge north of the farm with the whole sound below it. Sheep graze its sides. From the top you see every sail between the two ends of the strait. The wind never drops here, and men lower their voices without being asked.
sites.source: Storhaug at Gunnarshaug: 40-50 m across, 5-6 m high, the ship burial of summer 779 (Nordvegen History Centre). The man in it is named in no text; do not call him a king by name

sites.name: The Green Mound
sites.see: A second mound a little north of the first, lower and steeper, its turf still showing the cut lines of the sods in its first years. A boat lies under it with her stem to the south. For some summers a pole with a strip of red cloth stands on the top; later only the grass, and the name.
sites.source: Gronhaug at Bo: about 30 m across and 4 m high, a boat of about 15 m, a man's burial of 790-795 by tree rings (no.wikipedia 'Gronhaug'). The year 794 and the pole are the game's

sites.name: The stone and the two mounds
sites.see: Beside the hall a grey stone taller than four men leans a little, like a mast in a swell. Either side of it stand two more mounds, a great one and a lesser that the farm people call the cow mound. At the feasts the stone's foot is dark and wet and the ground is trodden. Children are told not to climb; they climb.
sites.source: The standing stone, 7.2 m (en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes'; snl.no): older than the church, its age not found (?). Flaghaug, 43 m across, and Kjellerhaug or Kuhaugen, 'the cow mound' (khm.uio.no). The stone's Mary name is Christian and later: nobody uses it here. King Ogvald and his cow: Olaf Trygvason's saga 71 (saga). Offerings at the stone are the game's

sites.name: The heath of the old mounds
sites.see: Above the farm the land rises to bare heather and bog cotton, and along the skyline stands a row of low mounds older than anyone's reckoning. Swine root between them, watched by boys with sticks. The open sea is grey to the west, the sound bright to the east. Wind, curlews, the grunt of pigs; in the king's years a stack of dry wood stands ready on the highest point.
sites.source: Rehaugane, the row of Bronze Age mounds on the heights (en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes'; snl.no). The battle of 953 among them, Blodeheia: Hakon the Good's saga 20 (saga). The swineherds are the spine's (holy_island)

sites.name: The skerries in the sound
sites.see: Low black rocks off the ness, wet to their tops at flood tide, white with birds. A man in a skin boat works along them with a net on a pole and a basket for eggs; seals watch him from the far side. Past them the channel narrows until two ships cannot pass without the crews seeing each other's faces.
sites.source: The narrow passage along Avaldsnes (en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes', 'Karmsund'). The fowler is npc_roles_793.json's (fowlers at Ogvaldsnes). Skrattasker, the skerry 'under water in flood tide': Olaf Trygvason's saga 70 (saga); which rock it is, is local tradition (?)

sites.name: The king's church
sites.see: A small church of upright timbers and a shingle roof, close by the hall with a trodden path between the two doors. The great stone leans toward its wall as if listening. Inside, one window, an altar with a cloth, a priest whose Norse has an English turn. Wax, damp wood, and on feast days more men outside than in.
sites.source: A church stands by the hall with a path to it at Easter 1023 (Saint Olaf's saga 127, saga). A wooden church is credited to Olaf Tryggvason without proof (en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes Church'); no trace has been reported (?). The year 998 is the game's, from his Easter here. English priests: Hakon's and the Olafs' bishops came from England (peoples/norse.md 10)

people.name: Thorleif
people.trait: A ship's chief of the west coast who farms in winter and sails in summer; was west over the sea in 793 and came home rich in things he has no use for.
people.want: Swords and a second ship; a name that outlasts him.
people.fear: A summer with nothing to show; his own crew's opinion.
people.voice: Understates everything: a sacked church is 'a good landing'. Laughs before he threatens.
people.looks: Early thirties, big, wind-burned, red-fair hair and beard, a blue tunic with tablet-woven braid, a silver neck ring, an axe with a long haft.
knows: what was taken west over the sea in 793 and who has it now
who buys people and where they go after
what a Frankish blade fetches at every landing north of the Eider
the sound, and which chiefs up the coast will be home this autumn

ties.note: sells him the people he takes
they know each other of old
nothing, as he sees it: he took the boy and sold him
his wife; she holds the keys and he has never yet won an argument about the store
the old steersman taught him the sound and still corrects him aloud
for the second ship, ordered and not paid for
the chief at the hall in the Vik, who answers to the Danes' king and thinks west-coast men are pirates with farms
the hilt smith in the Vik has six hilts waiting for blades Thorleif does not yet own
the same person
the dealer at the Slie sends him a tally stick by a Frisian to say what he owes, and means him to feel it
keeps a poet because a chief should, and pays him in rings and in not throwing him out
the caster at Ripa bought the gold off a book's boards from his crew and still owes the last ounce
has the Vik skipper's son at an oar, and sent him home quiet

lines.greet: A Frisian in a boat that size, this far north. Either you are brave or your steersman is lost. Sit down either way.
lines.greet_again: The small boat again. My men have a wager on how long she floats. I have my silver on you.
rumour: We made a good landing in the west. The men there keep their silver on a table and their door open. Strange people.
Asulf at Sliesthorp pays in silver for anyone who can walk. He feeds them better than I feed my crew, they tell me.
lines.ask_swords: Your king forbids you to sell me a sword. I do not see your king. I see you, and a boat with a ballast of stones.
lines.ask_boys: The English boys? They eat, they herd, they pray to the swine. Half a mark of silver each. Prayers I have enough of.
lines.saying: Praise the summer when the ship is in the boat-house.
lines.farewell: Go with a fair wind. If you meet a ship of mine at sea, shout your name early.

people.source: invented (the spine's cast.thorleif: trait, want, fear, voice and looks are the spine's words). Who raided Lindisfarne is not recorded (?): western Norway is the usual guess, from the Hordaland ships of 789 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787) and the church metalwork in graves along this coast. He is not the lord of the mounds, whose name is lost: the game makes him the old lord's sister's son

people.name: Gunnhild
people.trait: The woman with the keys: she runs the farm nine months of the year, weighs every piece of silver herself and forgets no weight she has ever read.
people.want: Grain and malt against a bad year; glass on her table; a burial for the old lord that the whole coast will speak of.
people.fear: A ship that does not come home at harvest; a winter with the corn bins showing their floors.
people.voice: Quick and exact. Asks a question, answers it herself, then waits to see if you dare correct her.
people.looks: Late twenties, straight-backed, fair hair knotted under a linen cloth, a strap dress hung from two oval brooches with beads between, keys and a folding scale at her belt; on her breast a third brooch, square and gilt, that was once the corner of a book.
knows: what is in the store and what it is worth in grain
the weight of an ounce, to a barleycorn
herbs: she keeps an angelica bed behind the hall
who on the farm is whose child, whatever is said
where the box of painted skins is, and that the pictures are the best thing in it

ties.note: her husband; she married the ship and got the man with it, she says
taught the English boy the farm's speech with a ladle, and later spoke for his freedom
the poet drinks her best ale and praises her husband
will not have the dealer sleep under her roof; he sleeps in his ship
wears on her breast the mount of a book from his church, and knows it came from a holy place
the ale-wife in the Vik sends her bead strings by any ship coming west and is paid in down (?)
asks the woman at the stone before any burial and any brewing, and pays in butter
the chief in the Vik sends to her, not to her husband, when he wants a thing kept safe (?)

lines.greet: You have come to trade. You will trade with me. My husband gives things away when he has had ale. What is in the boat?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. Your last malt was honest weight. Do not look pleased; I weighed it twice to be sure.
rumour: The old one will not see another winter. He must lie in a boat, with good things. I want glass for him. Clear glass.
The men came home with silver and two boys. I asked for corn. Nobody takes a corn bin in a raid.
The skins in that box have beasts biting their own tails in red and yellow. I keep them for the pictures.
lines.ask_brooch: It was on a board with skins behind it. The board burned well. The gold I kept. You look at it as a priest would.
lines.saying: A full bin is a better friend than a full hall.
lines.farewell: Bring grain next time. Silver I can get from any fool with a ship.

people.source: invented; the name is the chain lindisfarne_book's (its actor 'wife'), built Gunn- + -hildr (peoples/norse.md 7). Women keep the keys and the scales (peoples/norse.md 3). The brooch: church mounts from the British Isles recut as brooches lie in ninth-century graves of western Norway (spine, holy_island). The angelica bed is riddles_793.json's farm wife at Ogvaldsnes

people.name: Ofeig
people.trait: The old lord's steersman, too stiff now to row: he comes down to the strand each morning, asks who commands and what the errand is, and decides before the answer whether he likes you.
people.want: To be asked about weather and the sound; a gift for the hall brought up the path in plain sight, as it should be.
people.fear: Dying in the straw. A stranger's ship lost on his sound, which would be said to be his fault.
people.voice: Slow, in short pieces, with long looks at the sky between. Calls every man under fifty 'boy'.
people.looks: About sixty, bent, white beard to the chest, a sealskin cap, a grey wadmal cloak with a bone pin, a staff cut from an old oar, one hand missing two fingers.
knows: the sound: every rock, set and landmark from Bokn to the open sea in the north
tomorrow's weather, from the swell and the birds
who has passed this week, bound where, with what
how the lord of the Great Mound was buried: he carried the horse's halter

ties.note: taught him to steer; thinks he learned about half
they have argued about the same keel for thirty winters
says the poet was not at any fight he sings about
knew Ravn as a young man on this coast and will say so, if Ravn lets him
says no skipper of the Vik can find this sound without following a better ship; Bard has found it twenty times
they read the same swell each morning, agree, and resent it

lines.greet: Who commands here, and what is the errand? Speak up, boy. The gulls are louder than you.
lines.greet_again: You again. The boat is still afloat, then. I told them it would be. I did not believe it.
rumour: Swell from the north-west and no wind in it. By evening there will be wind in it. Stay on the strand tonight.
Three ships went north yesterday, low in the water. Two were Hordaland men. The third did not shout a name.
I held the horse when they laid the old lord in the Great Mound. It was a good horse. It did not want to go.
lines.teach_sound: Keep the tall stone over the boat-house roof until the black skerry opens. Then steer for the notch. Say it back to me.
lines.saying: Wits must he have who wanders wide, but all is easy at home.
lines.farewell: Keep the land on your left hand going south. If it is on your right, you are going north. Boy.

people.source: invented; the office is Saint Olaf's saga 123 (saga): the lord's man comes down in the morning to ask who commands and what the errand is. The weather-wise old seaman is texts_793.json's giver at this port. Name: Ofeigr, on a cross of Man (peoples/norse.md 7). The saying is Havamal 5 (Bellows 1923). The Great Mound's horse: avaldsnes.info, Storhaug

people.name: Hallgrim
people.trait: The hall's poet and keeper of its lays: vain, sharp, a memory like a net, and honest about exactly one thing, which is metre.
people.want: A ring for a verse, an audience that knows a good line, and news from abroad to make the next one from.
people.fear: Forgetting. A lord with no ear. A younger poet.
people.voice: Easy and mocking in talk; when he speaks verse his voice drops and slows and the hall goes quiet in spite of itself.
people.looks: Around forty, thin, dark for a Northman, a trimmed beard, a red cloak too good for him, an arm ring he turns while he thinks, a rune-cut stick thrust in his belt.
knows: the lays of the old kings and which parts he added
riddles: four of them cut on one stick, for a price
every man's nickname on the coast and how he got it
why the island is called Kormt, and who wades it

ties.note: makes the verses about him and is paid in rings and in not being thrown out
she counts what he drinks
the old man was at the fights and says the verses are wrong
has heard there is a blind Frisian who sings of old kings, and wants to know if he is any good
the poet of the Danes' hall; each has heard the other's best line and calls it borrowed (?)
the skipper of the Vik gives away riddles Hallgrim would have sold, and is forgiven because he brings news

lines.greet: A merchant. Good. Merchants have news and no opinions about verse. Sit. What has happened in the world?
lines.greet_again: My Frisian. I made a line about your boat. It is short, like the boat. You may not like it.
rumour: Thor wades this water every day on his way to the ash. That is why the fishing is bad on judgement days.
The lord in the Great Mound has two sets of playing pieces with him. Nobody to play. I call that a hard death.
They say a king named Ogvald took his cow to war and drank her milk for his health. It did not help in the end.
lines.sell_riddles: Four questions on one stick, eight pennies' weight. The answers are free, if you can find them.
lines.saying: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one's self; but a noble name will never die, if good renown one gets.
lines.farewell: Bring me a story from the south. A true one if you must.

people.source: invented: the skald of riddles_793.json and texts_793.json at this port (riddles r-gest-07a to 07d, bought for 8). The first skald with a name is Bragi the Old, ninth century: a hall poet in 793 is likely, his verses are not preserved. Thor and Kormt: Grimnismal 29. The gaming pieces: Storhaug. King Ogvald's cow: Olaf Trygvason's saga 71 (saga), set back here as a tale already old. The saying is Havamal 77 (Bellows 1923). Name: Hall- + -grimr

people.name: Odd
people.trait: The wright of the boat shore: builds by eye and hand with no measure but a knotted cord, and has never been pleased with a ship, his own least of all.
people.want: Straight oak, which the island does not grow; payment for the last ship before he lays the next keel.
people.fear: Green timber. A lord in a hurry. Seeing his work burned in a mound, which he has seen once.
people.voice: Hardly speaks. Answers a question about ships with a longer silence and then one word, usually 'no'.
people.looks: About forty-five, lean, grey-fair hair tied back with yarn, a leather apron stiff with tar, an adze on his shoulder, a knotted cord round his neck, sawdust in his eyebrows.
knows: what is wrong with your boat, at one look from the path
where good oak and pine can be had up the fjords, and from whom
how long a ship takes: a winter, and no shorter for silver
that the ship in the Great Mound was his master's best, and went into the ground nearly new

ties.note: builds for the hall, and is owed for the second ship
the only man whose opinion of a hull he will hear out
lets the English boy hold the planks; says he has steady hands for a swine-boy
for rivets from the smith in the Vik, a winter overdue (?)
Ravn once brought him an oak keel-piece from the south and has drunk on it since

lines.greet: Frisian boat. Broad. Lapped well enough. Your third strake on the steering side is weeping. No, the other third.
lines.greet_again: She still leaks where I said. You have not fixed it. You have put moss in it. That is not fixing.
rumour: There is no oak on this island. A ship comes here as trees in another ship. People forget that when they ask the price.
My master built the ship in the Great Mound. Planks three fingers thick. They put turf on her after six summers.
Thorleif wants twenty benches. He has silver for twelve. I have told him. He says build the twenty.
lines.ask_build: A winter. Bring the oak or pay for it. Come at the first day of summer. Not before. I do not like being watched.
lines.saying: The sea finds what the wright forgot.

people.source: invented; the trade from the ships in the mounds: planks 6 cm thick in the ship of 779, a boat built about 780 buried 790-795 (avaldsnes.info, Storhaug; no.wikipedia 'Gronhaug'). Name: Oddr, on a cross of Man (peoples/norse.md 7)

people.name: Cuthred
people.trait: A boy of Lindisfarena carried off in 793, set to herd swine on the heath: stubborn, watchful, and the kind who stops asking to go home and starts learning where everything is kept.
people.want: As a boy, that his name be read at Saint Cuthbert's altar so he is not counted dead. As a man, his freedom-ale, a plot, and news of Tidwine.
people.fear: Being sold on to the east, where nobody comes back from. Forgetting the psalms; he says them to the swine to keep them.
people.voice: As a boy, low and fast in English, looking over his shoulder. As a man, slow farm Norse with the odd Northumbrian word, and dry.
people.looks: As a boy: thirteen, thin, cropped hair growing out, a sack tunic, bare legs, a rope collar, a swine-stick notched down its length. As a man of forty: broad, weather-brown, a freedman's plain cloak, the same stick, new notches.
knows: which boys were taken and which ship each went in
everything said in the hall by men who think a thrall is furniture
the days: he notches every Sunday and every saint he remembers on his stick
in later years: the farm's beasts, its boundaries and its debts, better than the steward

ties.note: the younger boy taken with him; they herded together until Tidwine was sold on
his bishop, who has his name on a list of the lost
knows Tidwine's elder brother by sight from the island and will speak to nobody else first
hers to command; in time she speaks for his freedom
saw what Thorleif's men did in the church, and says nothing, yet
a brother of the house who is his mother's cousin (?)
the wright lets him hold the planks and says he has steady hands; it is the one kind word of his week

lines.greet: You are not one of them. Speak low. Are you from the Franks? Do you know the island of Saint Cuthbert?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. I cut a notch the day you left. That is forty Sundays. I count so that somebody does.
rumour: Tidwine cries at night and writes letters in the mud with his stick. They will sell him first. He can do a thing they want.
A man of the western islands carries water in the hall. He was taken later than us. He knows his abbot's name.
lines.ask_name: Tell the bishop Cuthred is alive and keeps the days. Have my name read at the altar. That costs you nothing.
lines.as_freedman: I brewed my freedom-ale and they all drank it. I have a wife, nine swine and a debt. I would not know the island now.
lines.saying: The swine do not mind the psalms. It is more than I can say for the hall.
lines.farewell: God keep you on the water. Say it back to me. I have not heard it said in two winters.

people.source: invented: one of the youths led away captive from Lindisfarne (Alcuin to Higbald, 793, MGH Epistolae IV no. 20); the spine's second swineherd (holy_island: 'two English boys herd swine; one was sold on'). The freedom-ale is the Gulathing law's custom (peoples/norse.md 3). Name: Cuth- + -red, both common in Northumbria

people.name: Arnstein
people.trait: King Harald's steward on the farm: a landed man's younger son who stood on the winning side in Hafrsfjord and has counted other men's cargoes ever since, fairly, slowly and aloud.
people.want: The king's share of everything that passes the sound, counted right; and to learn what northern goods fetch in the south, so that nobody sells the king short.
people.fear: The king's sons, each of whom thinks the farm will be his. A count that comes out wrong in front of the king.
people.voice: Level and patient. Says 'the king's' before every noun that matters, and repeats a number until you nod.
people.looks: A square grey-bearded man in his forties, a blue cloak with a silver ring pin, a sword he wears and has used, a tally stick and a folding scale at his belt, a stiff left knee.
knows: what is owed the king: five ounces of silver for every man bound for Iceland, and a share of every northern cargo
who has passed, bound where, and whose man the skipper is
where the king is this season and which son is with him
the day after Hafrsfjord: he saw the beaten ships go north with the wounded in the bilge

ties.note: holds the northern chief's sail ashore until the king's share of the Finn tribute is settled
the same man at his market in the Vik, where he says no king takes a share
the lawman of the Vik says law runs from the heath; Arnstein says it runs from the king
the sagas say the king outlawed Hrolf the Walker, whom the Franks call Rollo; Arnstein took the farm's share of what was left behind (saga) (?)

lines.greet: This is the king's farm and the king's sound. Who commands, whose man are you, and how many aboard?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian house. Your count was right last time. That is rarer than you would think.
rumour: The day after the fight in Hafrsfjord the beaten ships came through here rowing short. We let them pass. They were going far.
Men who will not have a king are selling land for a passage west. The king takes five ounces a head and wishes them wind.
A northern chief comes by each summer with teeth and hide rope and says he has no lord. The sound has one.
lines.ask_worth: Tell me what a pair of those teeth fetches in the south. The king likes to know what he is being given.
lines.saying: A man is master at home.
lines.farewell: Go in the king's peace as far as the sound runs. After that you are your own.

people.source: invented: the king's steward of the chain walrus_ivory (cards s06 and s13) and of skiringssal.json's ties. Harald Fairhair's hold on the farm after Hafrsfjord, and his dwelling here in old age, are Heimskringla, Harald Harfager's saga 40, 45 (saga); his own poet names Utstein, not this farm (dossier section 8). The Iceland toll: Ari, Islendingabok. The saying is Havamal 36 (Bellows 1923). Name: Arnsteinn, on a Norwegian stone (peoples/norse.md 7)

people.name: Thorir Sel
people.trait: King Olaf's bailiff at the farm: of low birth, polite in speech, showy in clothes, and exact about the king's law to the last sack when the sack is somebody else's.
people.want: To be seen doing the king's will; a better sail than his own; a seat near the high seat at Easter.
people.fear: Great men's kin, who remember what he was born. Being laughed at.
people.voice: Smooth and correct, never hurried; smiles while he takes things. Tells the same triumph again at each table, a little bigger.
people.looks: A well-fed man in middle age, hair combed and oiled, a cloak of scarlet with a silver clasp, rings on both hands, new shoes on a shingle beach.
knows: the king's bans: no corn, malt or meal north from 1022; no loading on a Sunday from 1024
who commands every ship on the strand and what she carries, by noon
what is in the king's corn stacks, and what a starving northerner will pay
where the king will keep Easter

ties.note: serves King Olaf, whose chiefs Cnut's silver is already buying; Thorir does not live to see how it ends
speaks of the Danish king's great men as pirates with titles (?)

lines.greet: Good morning. Who commands this ship, and what is her errand? Take your time. I have all day, and the king's seal.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian house. I remember the cargo. I remember every cargo. What is under the hides this time?
rumour: The king forbids corn, malt and meal to go north. I did not make the law. I only see that it is kept.
A northern man came for corn and bought it from thralls. I took the corn, and his sail was better than mine.
The king keeps Easter here. I am to stand before his table. Not sit, this year. Stand.
lines.boast: When we took the sail from him he wept.
lines.saying: The law is the king's, the sack is yours, and the difference is mine to settle.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and on a weekday.

people.source: Heimskringla, Saint Olaf's saga 123-124 (saga): 'of low birth', 'polite in speech, showy in clothes'; the seizure of Asbjorn's corn and the swap of sails in 1022; the boast 'When we took the sail from him he wept' (tr. S. Laing 1844) that cost him his head on the Thursday of Easter week 1023. The year he took office is not given: 1016 is the game's (?)

people.name: Alof
people.trait: The woman with a staff on the Karmsund: sits on the lesser mound by the great stone, reads the swell, and is asked before a burial, a brewing or a crossing west.
people.want: To be asked, and to be right; and one winter without the old steersman agreeing with her.
people.fear: A summer when the ship does not come home and she said it would.
people.voice: Dry, level, slower than the hall likes. Says what the sea is doing as if it were a neighbour's business.
people.looks: About forty-five, weather-brown, grey in dark hair under a hood, a grey cloak pinned with a bone pin, a staff shod with iron, a pouch of something that does not rattle.
knows: the swell in the sound and what it means for tomorrow
what is poured at the stone's foot at the turns of the year, and by whom
who lies in which of the old mounds, as her mother told it
which of the young men should not have gone west this summer

ties.note: the woman by the lake in the Vik says she guesses; Alof says anyone can see in flat water
they read the same swell each morning, agree, and resent it
Gunnhild asks her before any burial and any brewing, and pays in butter
knew him on this coast when he was young, and told him then that he would die among strangers; he thanked her

lines.greet: You stand downwind of the stone like a man who was told not to climb it. Good. I am not the stone. I only sit by it.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. The swell said a small boat. It did not say whose. It never gives names.
rumour: The stone leans a finger more than when I was a girl. When it falls, they say, that is the end of things. I have told the children not to climb. They climb.
The young men came home from the west with silver and soft-handed boys. The sea was quiet about it. The sea does not judge. I do, a little.
There is a woman by a lake in the Vik who says I guess. She sits by flat water. Anyone can see in flat water.
lines.saying: The sea tells you tomorrow. It is the day after that it keeps to itself.
lines.farewell: Go south with the land on your left hand. If you go west, ask me first. If you go home, ask your own god. He knows that water.

people.source: invented: the woman with a staff on the Karmsund of skiringssal.jorunn's tie. Seeresses with staffs are read from graves, a boat grave at Kaupang among them (the dossier of Skiringssal, not checked (?)); none is recorded here. Offerings at the stone are the game's (?); that the world ends when the stone touches the church wall is a legend of after the game (en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes'). The name is Alof (names_placeholder.json)

stories.title: The swineherds
stories.summary: Two boys from Saint Cuthbert's island herd swine on the heath above a heathen hall. One can write and will be sold east for it; the other counts Sundays on a stick and asks only that his name be read at the altar.
stories.picture: A bare heath with a row of low mounds on the skyline; two thin boys in sack tunics with sticks among rooting swine, one writing in the mud, the other looking straight out at the viewer.

beats.text: Bishop Higbald has the names of the boys who were taken and what he can pay: wax, wine, what silver the shrine has left. Cuthred and Tidwine are on the list. (Sets lf_knows_boys.)

A dealer at the summer market bought three English boys in the autumn of 793 and remembers the ship: a west-coast chief with a red beard, from the island Kormt, who kept a fourth because he could count. (Sets lf_trail_north.)

Thorleif's hall. On Gunnhild's breast is a brooch that was the corner of a book. He names his price before the ale is poured: half a mark of weighed silver a boy, or one good sword for the pair. (Sets lf_boy_found.)

A thrall of the islands' speech, taken at Hi, carries water in the hall. To a man under his abbot's protection he tells what he tells nobody: which boy went in which ship, and that the one who writes is to go east. (Sets lf_trail_north.)
Both boys are with the swine. Tidwine wants home and says so in Latin when he forgets himself. Cuthred asks one thing that costs nothing: his name read at the altar, so that he is not counted dead.

beats.when: year >= 796 and year < 807 and not flag.lf_ransom_paid
beats.text: One boy with the swine. Tidwine went east with Asulf's lot the summer after the new mound was raised. Cuthred has a notch for the day.
Asulf remembers every lot: the English boy who could tally went on with a Svea, because a Christian cannot be sold south to the Franks.
The name is read at the altar, or the boy himself walks up the sand at low water. Either way the bishop strikes a line from his list.

endings.how: You paid a mark of weighed silver before the summer of 796 and carried both boys to Lindisfarena.
endings.text: They go up the sand at low water. Tidwine runs. Cuthred walks, counting the notches on his stick aloud, and is three days out.
endings.reward: Sets lf_ransom_paid, then clears it; the bishop's wax and wine to the value of the ransom and half again; Beornwine yours for life; a deed of mercy known in every Northumbrian house. Sets og_boys_home.

endings.how: You gave Thorleif a Frankish sword for both boys.
endings.text: The boys come home on a blade that will go west again next summer in the hand that took them. Higbald thanks you and does not ask the price. Aldger asks, every fast day.
endings.reward: The boys home as above; sets sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known; Thorleif friendly; Aldger's heart falls. Sets og_boys_home and og_sword_paid.

endings.how: You could not or would not pay, but carried Cuthred's name to the bishop.
endings.text: His name is read at Saint Cuthbert's altar on the saint's day. Cuthred stays, is freed in time, and brews his freedom-ale. Every heir of your house who lands here is met on the strand by a broad man with a notched stick.
endings.reward: Sets og_cuthred_friend: Cuthred tells you what is said in the hall, on every visit, for fifty years; standing at Lindisfarena a little up; the unlock ogvaldsnes.cuthreds_word.

endings.how: You came after 796, or did nothing.
endings.text: Tidwine is at Birka, keeping a Svea's tallies. The trail goes on east, and it is a long one.
endings.reward: Nothing here. The spine's later beats at Sliesthorp and Birka stay open (cast.holmfast).

stories.reward: Two boys home, or one friend for life on a heathen farm who remembers which you chose.

stories.title: A blade for a tusk
stories.summary: Thorleif wants Frankish swords more than silver and says so in front of his whole hall. The law that forbids the sale is a thousand miles south; the man who wants the sword is across the fire.
stories.picture: Firelight in a long hall: a big red-bearded man holding a pair of walrus tusks across his knees, looking at the plain sword on a Frisian merchant's belt, the benches behind him leaning in to hear.

beats.text: A blade may be sold to a count's man and to no stranger. A dealer who asks no questions wants silver by weight.
The toll man's search. Whatever is under the ballast stays there, or does not. (Sets sw_ran_blades or sw_marked.)
Thorleif names his price aloud so the benches hear it: a pair of tusks for a sword, or an English boy, or thirty ounces of silver for three. He laughs first. (Sets sw_buyer_known.)
Gunnhild weighs the sword in her hands like a ham and says her husband will pay too much, and that she will see he pays it in things she has too many of.
The smith here cannot make such a blade and knows it. He will buy a bare one to hilt, quietly, for iron and whetstones, and tell nobody whose boat it came in.
A smith in the Vik fits northern hilts to Frankish blades. He has heard there is a Frisian who comes to the Kormt sound.
A ship comes in from the west with a wounded man aboard. The sword on the chief's knee has a hilt you have seen before.
At the Slie a Dane pays double in weighed silver for the same blade, and the dealer Asulf pays in people. Thorleif pays in tusks, and says his is the honest price.
At the Vik's market a Dane sells the news that Thorleif is drowned and his widow selling swords cheap. He is not drowned. He was wet.

endings.how: You brought him swords and took tusks, silver or people for them.
endings.text: Thorleif has his blades and his second ship is paid for. You are a guest for life in a hall that is feared on four coasts. In later years the swords come back across the sea without you.
endings.reward: Sets og_sword_paid and sw_buyer_known; walrus ivory worth three times the sword's price in the south; Thorleif a fast friend; the unlock ogvaldsnes.guest_seat. Aldger's heart falls, and the next Frankish search is harder if sw_marked.

endings.how: You refused the swords and brought grain, malt and bar iron, and said why.
endings.text: Thorleif laughs and says a Frisian is a man who sells you the plough and keeps the edge. Gunnhild fills your boat herself. The hall thinks you careful, which here is not quite praise.
endings.reward: Gunnhild a fast friend; goods from the store at her price; no mark against you in Francia. Sets og_gunnhilds_trade.

endings.how: You carried Thorleif's name and his price to the count's men at Dorestad.
endings.text: The count's clerk writes it down. Nothing is done; the north is far. But a Frisian skipper tells it at Sliesthorp, and by the next summer the hall on Kormt has heard.
endings.reward: Standing in the Rhine delta up; a deed of the king's service. Thorleif wary, and every west-coast ship you meet at sea has heard a little.

stories.reward: A buyer in the north by name, tusks for the altars of Cologne, and a choice your crew will not let you forget.

stories.title: The painted skins
stories.summary: A gospel book lies in a box in a heathen store, its boards burned and its gold on a woman's breast, the leaves kept because the beasts in them are finely drawn. In that hall only the merchant can know what it is worth here and what it is worth to the house it came from.
stories.picture: A dim log storehouse: a woman with keys holding up one painted leaf to the light of the door, knotted beasts in red and yellow glowing on it, a square gilt brooch on her breast, soapstone pots behind.

beats.text: A scribe at the minster will price any book you describe: so many calves, so many months of a man's eyes. (Sets bk_knows_worth.)
Gunnhild shows the box. The leaves are whole. Thorleif wants swords or three hundred pennies' weight; she wants to keep the pictures.
You alone in the hall know both prices. To say the true one is to raise it; to keep quiet is to buy a year of a scribe's life for the price of a cloak.

The box has passed to a daughter of the house. Some leaves are gone: one lines a child's cap, one was given away at a wedding for its red beast. What is left is still more book than most churches own.
The brothers know their own hand. A leaf laid on the desk is read aloud before anyone asks how you came by it.
You told them what it was and let it go. A summer later the man who took it owes you for a true word, and pays.
At the Vik's market leaves of the same kind lie on a dealer's cloth and are sold as patterns for ribbon. A weaver took two.
At Ripa a goldsmith wraps his brooch moulds in nine leaves of another book, because they take the heat well.

endings.how: You said nothing of its worth, paid the heathen price and carried it to a church.
endings.text: The book goes home, or to York. The house that sold it never learns what it sold. You do not mention the price at either end.
endings.reward: Sets bk_carried and lf_ransom_paid; the difference between two prices, which is most of a ship; Beornwine reads from it at anchor on the way.

endings.how: You told Gunnhild what the leaves are worth to the men who made them.
endings.text: She doubles the price and then, because you told her, halves it again for you alone. From that day nothing from over the sea is sold from her store until you have seen it.
endings.reward: Sets og_gunnhilds_trade: first sight of every church thing that comes to this farm, at her price; the book for a fair sum.

endings.how: You left it where it was.
endings.text: The leaves stay in the box for the pictures. In eighty years they are a cap lining, a wedding gift, a handful of bright scraps in a grave.
endings.reward: Nothing but the knowledge. Told at any scriptorium, it earns a scribe's long silence and a small gift for the telling.

stories.reward: A book bought back, or a woman's trust and first sight of everything the ships bring home.

stories.title: Glass for the mound
stories.summary: The old lord of the ness is dying and will be laid in a boat on the ridge. Gunnhild wants one thing in the grave that no other hall on the coast could put there: a cup of clear glass from over the sea.
stories.picture: A boat sunk in a trench on a windy ridge, half covered with turf; a woman in a strap dress setting a thin glass beaker among wooden bowls and bedding at the dead man's side, the sound grey below.

beats.text: The old lord sits propped in the high seat and does not speak. Gunnhild asks for glass: a tall clear cup, the best you can find, by the time the corn is cut next year.
Glass cups of the English kind, thin as a leaf, are to be had where the Frisians sell on the Ouse. One good one costs what a sword costs. Also at Dorestad and Lundenwic.
Odd is fitting new rowlocks to a boat he built fourteen winters ago. He says nothing about what it is for. Everybody knows.
The boat is in the ground with the old man in her on a bed, bowls and hooped buckets round him, a hanging on the wall of the chamber. Your cup can go in at his hand, before the turf.
The mound is closed. Gunnhild takes the cup anyway, pours ale from it on the turf, and puts it on her own table.

endings.how: You brought the glass in time and gave it as a gift.
endings.text: The cup goes into the ground at the old lord's hand. Hallgrim puts the Frisian's gift in the burial verse, between the horse and the bed. A gift asks a gift: you have a seat on the guests' bench for as long as the hall stands.
endings.reward: Sets og_grave_gift; the unlock ogvaldsnes.guest_seat for you and your heirs; every person of the farm friendly at the least; a pair of walrus tusks in return.

endings.how: You brought the glass and named a price.
endings.text: Gunnhild pays it, by weight, without a word. The cup goes into the grave all the same. You are a man who sold a dead lord his cup, and the coast hears it so.
endings.reward: Three times the cup's price in weighed silver; Gunnhild cool for some years; no seat.

endings.how: You came after the turf was laid, and gave the cup.
endings.text: Ale is poured from it on the mound and it stands on the hall table after. Ofeig says a late guest is better than a liar.
endings.reward: Gunnhild friendly; goods from the store at her price for that season. Sets og_gunnhilds_trade.

stories.reward: Guest-right in the hall for the house, and your gift in a grave that will be opened eleven hundred years on.

stories.title: The striped sail
stories.summary: In 1022 the king forbids corn to go north while the north starves, and his bailiff Thorir Sel enforces it with pleasure. The next skipper he stops on the strand, after Asbjorn of Halogaland, is you.
stories.picture: A shingle beach at morning: a plump man in a scarlet cloak pointing at sacks in the hold of a merchant ship, armed men behind him, an old patched sail lying on the stones beside a fine striped one being carried away.

beats.text: A northern ship lies stripped on the strand: twenty men, no corn, and an old patched sail where a striped one hung. The master, Asbjorn, says little and looks at the hall for a long time.

beats.when: year >= 1022 and year <= 1023 and (hold.barley >= 1 or hold.malt >= 1 or hold.rye >= 1 or hold.flour >= 1)
beats.text: Thorir Sel comes down in the morning in new shoes. Who commands, what errand, and what is under the hides? Corn bound north is the king's by forfeit. He admires your sail.
At the autumn feasting Thorir tells the story of the northerner's sail again, and it has grown: 'When we took the sail from him he wept.'

Easter week, the king at table, Thorir standing before him telling it once more. A man in a hood comes in from the ante-room. The head lands on the board in front of the king, and the body at his feet.
The Sunday after: the sound black with ships, and Erling of Sola's men standing in two rows from the church door to the hall so that the king must walk between them.

endings.how: You gave up the corn and kept your sail by a gift of silver to Thorir himself.
endings.text: The bailiff is gracious. He remembers you kindly, for one winter, which is all the winters he has.
endings.reward: The corn lost; Thorir friendly until Easter 1023; no mark with the king's men. Sets og_paid_thorir.

endings.how: You hid the corn under hides and salt and slipped the sound at night with a pilot.
endings.text: North of the Stad a sack of malt is worth what a cow was. Chiefs there remember a southern ship that came when the king's law said none should.
endings.reward: Four times the price for grain in the north that year; a deed of mercy among the northern men; the king's bailiffs wary of your house. Sets og_ran_corn.

endings.how: You were in the hall on the Thursday of Easter week and said what you saw, plainly, when asked.
endings.text: You are named as a witness before the king and before Erling's men both, and neither side finds you lied. In a country where proof is an oath, a stranger whose word stood between two great men is worth knowing.
endings.reward: Standing up along the whole west coast; a deed of honest witness; lodging in the hall under the new bailiff. Sets og_easter_witness.

stories.reward: A famine's price for grain, or the king's bailiff's favour, or a name as a witness: not all three.

works.name: A gift into the Green Mound
works.what: When the old lord is laid in his boat, a stranger's gift set beside him: a glass cup, a turned bowl, a hanging. Given before the whole household, and remembered by it.
works.needs: To be here between the corn harvest and the winter nights of 794, with a thing fit for a lord in the boat.
works.gives: Guest-right in the hall (the unlock ogvaldsnes.guest_seat); a deed of honour among the old gods' people on this coast.
works.picture: A hand setting a thin glass beaker among wooden bowls in the bottom of a boat, turf sods stacked ready at the trench's edge.
works.source: The grave goods of Gronhaug: a piece of a very fine glass beaker called English, hooped vessels, turned bowls, tapestry and bedding (no.wikipedia 'Gronhaug'). That a foreign merchant gave any of it is the game's

works.name: A boat-house of your own
works.what: A long low house of turf and stone on the boat shore, open at the sea end, with rollers of pine laid down its floor. Your ship can stand dry in it over a winter under Odd's eye.
works.needs: Guest-right in the hall, or the bailiff's leave in the king's years; turf and stone are here, the roof timber you must bring.
works.gives: A ship may winter here and be careened and repaired at half the cost (store, repair, careen); you may sail north from here at the first day of summer, a month before any ship from the south.
works.picture: A low turf-roofed shed open to a grey sound, a ship's stem showing from its dark mouth, snow on the roof.
works.source: Boat-houses are the ordinary winter shelter of ships on this coast, from before the game's years to after it (?); none has been reported at this farm. Ships go into the water after Easter and come out in October (Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 2.11)

works.name: A share in the salt boiling
works.what: A second iron pan and a season's driftwood and peat for the thrall who boils sea water at the workshop ground. The lord's household takes two parts of the salt and you the third.
works.needs: Gunnhild's good will, or the steward's in later years; bar iron for the pan.
works.gives: Coarse grey salt at source on every call (buy_at_source), enough to salt a boatload of fish or butter going south.
works.picture: A wide shallow iron pan steaming over a driftwood fire on the shore, a man raking white crust to its edge, smoke blowing flat along the water.
works.source: Salt making in the workshop area, about 200 to 1000 (Nordvegen History Centre, research page). The iron pan and the shares are the game's (?)

works.name: Wood for the beacon
works.what: A stack of tarred pine on the highest point of the heath, roofed with turf against the rain, and a watchman's hut beside it. When ships of war come up the coast it is lit, and the next one north answers.
works.needs: The king's steward friendly; pine and tar, which you can bring.
works.gives: Warning: while it stands, a card of raiders or a king's fleet at this port is known to you a day early, and the steward counts you among the men of the sound.
works.picture: A tall stack of dark wood on a bare hilltop among old mounds, a small turf hut beside it, a second point of fire far away along the coast at dusk.
works.source: King Hakon's law of beacons on the hills, each to be seen from the next: Heimskringla, Hakon the Good's saga 21 (saga; chapter from memory (?)). In 953 the sons of Eric landed here all the same

works.name: A door and a bell for the king's church
works.what: An oak door with iron bands and a small hand bell of the Irish kind for the wooden church by the hall, which has had a hide across its doorway since it was built.
works.needs: The church standing; oak brought from the south or bought up the fjords; a bell from Dyflin or England.
works.gives: The priest's good word with the king's men; sanctuary here is honoured for your crew; alms given in your house's name on Saint Olaf's day after 1031.
works.picture: A small upright-timber church with a new pale oak door standing open, a priest ringing a hand bell on the step, a great grey stone leaning over the roof.
works.source: The church by the hall is Saint Olaf's saga 127 (saga, of 1023), and is credited to Olaf Tryggvason without proof (en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes Church') (?). Hand bells of sheet iron are the Irish and English churches' in these years. The gift is the game's

ships.note: A four- or six-oared farm boat off the strand, of pine, light enough for two men to drag. Every household on the sound has more than one, and a widow or an heir will sell.
ships.picture: A small slim clinker boat drawn up on shingle beside a turf boat-house, oars laid across her thwarts, nets drying on a rack behind.
ships.source: A smaller boat lay with the ship in the mound of 779 (avaldsnes.info, Storhaug); story/ships_793.json builds this class here

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: Odd's kind of ship, and his successors': a fifteen-metre boat for oars and sail that will carry a cargo or a crew. The oak comes from up the fjords and is counted in the price. Order at the first day of summer, take her the summer after.
ships.picture: A lean double-ended hull on rollers under an open sky, half planked, a man with an adze on the keel and a steaming trough beside him.
ships.source: The Gronhaug boat, about 15 m, built about 780 (no.wikipedia 'Gronhaug'); story/ships_793.json

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: A ship of twenty benches like the one in the Great Mound. No stranger gets one without guest-right in the hall, or in the king's years the bailiff's leave, and she takes every wright on the sound a full winter.
ships.picture: A long low oared ship with a high curled stem lying in the sound under the farm, shields along her side, a striped sail furled on the yard.
ships.source: The Storhaug ship: keel about 22 m, some 27 m in all, planks 6 cm thick, buried 779 (avaldsnes.info, Storhaug). A warship of twenty benches lay here in 1023 (Saint Olaf's saga 124, saga)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The deep, broad cargo ship of the later years, built of pine in the fjords north of here and sold along the coast road. Asbjorn's corn ship of 1022, with twenty men, was one of the kind.
ships.picture: A short high-sided ship with a deep open hold and one tall mast, sacks being handed down into her from a shingle beach.
ships.source: A cargo ship with twenty men here in 1022 (Saint Olaf's saga 123, saga); Skuldelev 1, pine, built in Sogn about 1030 (peoples/norse.md 6); story/ships_793.json lists this port. The start year 1000 is the game's (?)

sayings.text: Kormt and Ormt and the Kerlaugs twain shall Thor each day wade through, when dooms to give he forth shall go to the ash-tree Yggdrasil.
sayings.source: Grimnismal 29, tr. H. A. Bellows 1923 (from memory: check the wording before it ships (?)). Kormt is the island's own name
Havamal 41, tr. H. A. Bellows 1923 (texts_793.json): the whole trade of this place in five words

sayings.text: Give praise to the day at evening, to ice when it is crossed, to ale that is drunk.
sayings.source: Havamal 81, tr. H. A. Bellows 1923 (texts_793.json), shortened: what Ofeig says to any skipper who is sure of tomorrow's wind

sayings.text: The live man catches the cow.
sayings.source: Havamal 70, tr. H. A. Bellows 1923: said here with a nod at the cow mound

sayings.text: He made great sacrifices to a cow which he had with him wherever he went, and considered it good for his health to drink her milk.
sayings.source: Heimskringla, Olaf Trygvason's saga 71, tr. S. Laing 1844 (saga): of King Ogvald, who gave the ness its name. The period's own joke, told deadpan by a one-eyed guest

sayings.text: A good landing: nobody was home but the owners.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: the Northman's understatement (BRIEF.md, tone)

sayings.text: Whoever holds the sound need not go to market. The market comes past his door and slows down.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the narrow passage along the farm (en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes')

sayings.text: When we took the sail from him he wept.
sayings.source: Heimskringla, Saint Olaf's saga 124, tr. S. Laing 1844 (saga): Thorir Sel's boast at the king's table, Easter 1023. Use only from 1022
Heimskringla, Olaf Trygvason's saga 71, tr. S. Laing 1844 (saga): King Olaf, throwing out the meat the one-eyed guest gave his cooks. Use only from 998

sayings.text: The lord's man asks who commands. The lord's wife knows already what is in the hold.

easter_eggs.text: If your glass cup went into the Green Mound in 794, Hallgrim's verse says it will 'wait in the dark for a guest who digs'. A piece of a very fine English glass beaker was found in the mound in 1902, and the mound was opened again in the summer of 2026.

Hallgrim says the dead lord in the Great Mound has two sets of playing pieces, amber and coloured glass, and a cake of wax with a mark scratched on it like two crossed sticks. Nobody at the farm knows what the mark means. A Christian crewman goes very quiet.
easter_eggs.source: Storhaug, 779: two sets of gaming pieces and a wax cake marked with a cross, unexplained and no proof of a Christian (avaldsnes.info, Storhaug-kongen)

easter_eggs.text: Ask anyone what is in the great mound by the stone and they shrug: an old one, from before. Children say a giant's neck ring. They are right, and nobody will know it for a thousand years.
easter_eggs.source: Flaghaug, levelled in 1835: a neck ring of 600 g of gold from the 200s (en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes'). Nobody in the game's years may know it (dossier section 8)

easter_eggs.text: Each generation of your house can measure the stone's lean with a hand against the hall post behind it. Ofeig says it leans a finger more than when he was a boy, and that when it falls the world is over. Later a priest says the same of the church wall, and looks thoughtfully at the stone's top.
easter_eggs.source: The stone leans to within 9.2 cm of the church wall; the world ends when it touches, and priests are said to have chipped the top (?) (en.wikipedia 'Avaldsnes'; avaldsnes.info, the church). A legend of after the game, hinted at only

easter_eggs.text: At Easter 998 an old man in a broad hat with one eye sits on the guests' bench and has something to tell of every land. If you are in the hall that night you may ask him one question about any port on the chart, and the answer is true. In the morning he is gone, and the cooks have two fat pieces of beef nobody remembers buying.
easter_eggs.source: Heimskringla, Olaf Trygvason's saga 71, tr. S. Laing 1844 (saga): the guest who 'had something to tell of every land'. The question is the game's

easter_eggs.text: In the spring of 998 the fowler will not go near one skerry. He says men walked round and round on it all one night in a fog that lay nowhere else, and that he heard them until the tide came in.
easter_eggs.source: Heimskringla, Olaf Trygvason's saga 70 (saga): Eyvind Kelda and his crew, blinded in their own mist, walked 'round and round in a circle upon the island' and were left bound on Skrattasker

easter_eggs.text: After 932 ships going north past the farm dip their yards off a new mound on the mainland shore, half a morning's row up the sound. The steward says that is where the king lies who made one kingdom of all this, and that he was carried there from this hall.
easter_eggs.source: Harald's burial at Haugar on the Karmsund: Harald Harfager's saga 45 (saga). Dipping the yard is the game's (?)

easter_eggs.text: Cuthred's stick, if you ask to see it, has a deeper notch every seventh mark and a cross-cut for each saint he remembers. In 794 he is three days out. By 830 he is eleven days out and will not be told.
easter_eggs.source: invented; a tally of days kept without a calendar drifts, and the Easter tables were the monks' own hard problem (Bede, The Reckoning of Time)

unlocks.what: A seat on the guests' bench
unlocks.how: Give the glass for the Green Mound in 794, or bring Thorleif what he asks, or in later years give the lord or the king's steward a gift worth a sword.
unlocks.gives: Lodging in the hall and leave to trade from the store on every visit (lodge, audience, market) without a new gift; leave to order a ship of twenty benches. Passes to your heir at half strength. Sets og_grave_gift or og_sword_paid.

unlocks.how: Hire him or his successor as pilot twice and say the marks back to him without a mistake.
unlocks.gives: learn: the Kormt sound from Bokn to the open sea without a pilot, by day or in a light night. The same knowledge as unlock_pilot_karmsund in the chain walrus_ivory.

unlocks.how: Carry his name to the bishop at Lindisfarena, or ransom him and have him choose to stay.
unlocks.gives: Sets og_cuthred_friend: on every visit until 846 he tells you what was said in the hall about you, your goods and the next ship due (ask_news at its best, free). He will speak for you before the lord.

unlocks.how: Bring grain or malt in a hungry year, or tell her the true worth of the painted skins.
unlocks.gives: Sets og_gunnhilds_trade: goods from the store at her price (about a fifth under), and first sight of every thing from over the sea before a dealer from the Vik sees it.

unlocks.how: Pay him eight pennies' weight of silver, or tell him a story from the south that he has not heard.
unlocks.gives: give_riddle: the four riddles r-gest-07a to r-gest-07d, cut on one stick (riddles_793.json).

unlocks.what: A winter berth on the boat shore
unlocks.gives: Your ship may lie here from the winter nights to the first day of summer; repairs at half cost; a start north a month before the southern ships.

unlocks.what: The first signing for a heathen deckhand
unlocks.how: From 995: bring a heathen crewman to the king's priest, with the man's own consent and a gift of wax.
unlocks.gives: The ship may sail from King Olaf's harbours with a mixed crew; the man may eat and deal with Christians and still keep his own counsel. His heart falls a little if he was pressed.
